title: Bereshit: two creation accounts (Genesis 1–2)
hookLine: chapter one is vast and ordered, chapter two close and earthy; tradition holds both
tomorrow: Bereshit: one person, a whole world

lines: A DRONE SHOT OF A CROWDED SQUARE.
A CLOSE-UP WITH FLOUR ON ONE CHEEK.
cards: Two photographs of the same person sit side by side. One is taken from a drone, high above a crowded square: a tiny figure, part of a vast pattern.
The other is a close-up: the lines around the eyes, a smudge of flour on one cheek. Which one is true? Both.
They just stand in different places. The first two chapters of Genesis are like that. Creation is told, then told again, and the two tellings don't sound alike.

teach.b: Chapter one is the drone shot. Vast and ordered: light, sky, sea and land, plants, lights in the sky, fish and birds, animals. Six days, each ending, and there was evening and there was morning.
God speaks, and it is. Human beings come last, all at once: "male and female created He them," in the image of God. Chapter two is the close-up.
Suddenly the story is on the ground. No plants yet, no rain; a mist waters the earth.
God, now called by a different name, the LORD God, "formed man of the dust of the ground," and breathes into his nostrils the breath of life.

In Hebrew the human is adam and the ground is adamah; the two words sound alike. Then a garden, a river, animals brought to be named, and a partner built from his side. Two tellings, two orders, even two names of God.
People read this in different ways. Some modern scholars say two older sources were woven together. Traditional commentators read one Torah showing two sides of the same truth.
The midrash notices the two names: one stands for God's justice, the other for God's mercy, and the world was made with both, because it couldn't stand on either alone.
A modern teacher, Rabbi Joseph Soloveitchik, wrote of two Adams: one who builds and masters the world, and one who is lonely and longs for a companion and for God.
Every person, he said, is both. Read this way, the Torah doesn't choose between the drone and the close-up.
It keeps both photographs, side by side.

how: Jewish readers study Genesis 1 and 2 side by side in the portion of Bereshit, often with midrash on the two names of God and modern commentary on the two accounts.

o: the seventh day, when God rested from work
in the beginning: the Torah's opening portion
the garden where the first humans lived

p: justice and mercy, the midrash says

s: Genesis tells creation once, in one order
chapter one and chapter two tell it differently, even with different names of God.
in chapter one, humans are created last
male and female together, in the image of God.
Soloveitchik wrote of two Adams in every person
one who builds and masters, one who is lonely and longs.

games.q: you're reading Genesis and notice chapter two retells creation differently from chapter one. what does Jewish tradition do?
o: pick the one that seems more accurate.
hold both and ask what each shows.
games.why: tradition holds both. the midrash reads two names as justice and mercy; Soloveitchik reads two sides of every person.

practice: First, the drone shot: see yourself from high above, one small person in a huge, ordered world, and stay there a few breaths. Then come down close: your breath in your nostrils, your hands, the dust and warmth of you.
Don't choose; let both be true at once.

wordCard.voice: Bereshit. The first portion, where creation is told twice, vast and close, and the tradition keeps both.

orig.note: Hebrew: a human being; the word sounds like adamah, the ground.

carryVoice: Your line: both are true. Two photographs, one person, and neither one is wrong. See you tomorrow.
